item.title: I stopped using Wi-Fi smart plugs after switching to Zigbee relays, and my automations never fail anymore
item.itunes:title: I stopped using Wi-Fi smart plugs after switching to Zigbee relays, and my automations never fail anymore
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you walk into a room, issue a voice command or trigger an automation, and nothing happens, you might start to think, "Why did I ever pivot to a smart home?" You check your phone only to find a stubborn Wi-Fi smart plug sitting offline, choked by router IP lease drops or lost cloud connectivity. For years, consumers flooded their home networks with cheap cloud-tethered 2.4GHz Wi-Fi smart plugs. Every single plug runs its own TCP/IP handshake, and it clogs your router's client table.

Luckily, there's a fix. Pull out the Wi-Fi plugs and rip out the cloud applications, and you can transition to a dedicated local mesh infrastructure powered by Zigbee relays and in-wall micro-modules. Wi-Fi is the wrong protocol for static IoT devices. By shifting your smart home foundation to a local self-healing Zigbee relay, you eliminate network congestion, banish cloud dependency, and build automations that execute with instantaneous, unyielding reliability.

By  Ayush Pande

Why does Wi-Fi seem to fall so far behind?

Wi-Fi just wasn't built for smart homes

Wi-Fi smart plugs seem to fail at scale compared to dedicated low-power mesh networks due to the actual architecture; there's a major difference between Wi-Fi and Zigbee Mesh. Wi-Fi routers are designed for high-throughput traffic like streaming or file transfers rather than hundreds of tiny idle smart plugs spamming keep-alive packets. When you expand your smart home and add 30+ Wi-Fi IoT devices, this quickly overwhelms residential routers and can cause random disconnections. Any standard 2.4GHz router is absolutely overloaded when you're connecting so many different devices.

By contrast, a self-healing Zigbee mesh behaves very differently. Zigbee does operate on the same 2.4GHz ISM band, but it uses an IEEE 802.15.4 low-power mesh protocol. Every mains-powered relay or switch acts as a routed node, actively strengthening the mesh network. If one path drops, signals automatically reroute through neighboring devices instantly.

What are the perks of Zigbee?

You get so many benefits

Zigbee relays, in particular, give you a hidden advantage in wall power. Moving from bulky plug-in adapters to discrete Zigbee relays can really change the game for your smart home. You get true in-wall fixture integration rather than bulky plastic blocks sticking out of wall outlets. Compact Zigbee micro-modules wire directly behind existing light switches or inside fixture boxes, keeping your physical aesthetic clean.

Decoupled switch control also helps protect your smart bulbs. Advanced Zigbee relays support decoupled mode, letting you cut physical power to smart bulbs while still exposing the switch state as an event trigger in Home Assistant. This means you can prevent family members from accidentally cutting power to bulbs so your automations stay intact, while other household members can still use the switch as normal.

You also get fully air-gapped local control, as Zigbee relays run entirely within your local Home Assistant or Zigbee2MQTT stack without ever falling back to external servers or third-party apps.

How to get started with switching over to Zigbee

There are some hurdles to overcome

Building a robust mesh comes with practical hurdles, so watch for these challenges before deploying. You have to build router density first. Because Zigbee relies on mains-powered devices to act as repeaters, ensure you install plugged-in relays or smart switches before adding any battery-powered sensors to build a strong mesh foundation. If you rely on battery-powered sensors to repeat signals, this won't work, and your messages won't be strong enough.

You have to manage any channel interference. Managing 2.4GHz Wi-Fi channel overlap can be a bit tricky. You should avoid channels that clash with your chosen Zigbee coordinator channels, such as Wi-Fi channels 1, 6, or 11 versus Zigbee channels 11, 15, 20, and 25.

If you're looking to migrate from Wi-Fi plugs, the first step is deploying a dedicated Zigbee coordinator. Set up a robust USB coordinator running ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT locally.

Next, you should install all of your mains-powered relays by replacing or supplementing your smart plugs with in-wall relay Zigbee modules to anchor your mesh network. This way, any other devices that you add to your network will have this strong foundation.

And lastly, it's time to cut the cloud cord. Pair all of your new devices directly to your local coordinator so that they don't have to phone home to any third-party applications. You can block their access at the router level if any stray Wi-Fi variants exist, then rewrite your Home Assistant automations around local Zigbee triggers instead.

Stop dealing with network drops

Local is superior

A smart home shouldn't require troubleshooting network drops every time you turn on a light. Moving away from congested Wi-Fi smart plugs to robust local Zigbee relays transforms your home automation stack. It means you no longer have to deal with failing Wi-Fi smart sockets or worry about other members of your family hitting your light switches.

item.title: I replaced Windows' Snipping Tool with ShareX for screenshots, but the best part is everything else it can do
item.itunes:title: I replaced Windows' Snipping Tool with ShareX for screenshots, but the best part is everything else it can do
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Snipping Tool on Windows is one of the most useful built-in apps Microsoft makes. I never used to touch it, but since it got modernized in Windows 11, it's become a very solid option for taking screenshots and recording my screen. Occasionally, though, it can become buggy and not work as intended, so I set out to replace it.

The best way to do it ended up being ShareX, a free and open-source tool that's not only great for taking screenshots, but it can do a whole lot more than that, too. Even if you think Snipping Tool works well for you, I highly recommend checking it out.

It does everything you'd expect

Screenshots, videos, and more

At its core, taking screenshots is a pretty simple feature, but there's still room for building on top of that, and ShareX goes above and beyond to perfect the act of taking and editing a screenshot. For one thing, the app as a while is very lightweight, and the action of taking a screenshot feels even more responsive than with the built-in Snipping Tool.

One notable benefit of using ShareX is the precise selection tool, too. ShareX shows you a very zoomed in view of the pixels around your mouse cursor, so you can crop your screenshot perfectly without editing it later. And speaking of editing, the screenshot UI in ShareX lets you add all kinds of elements even before the screenshot is saved, so you can highlight a specific element, overlay another emoji, add emoji, or even a fake mouse cursor. This can be particularly helpful for making tutorials, for example.

Of course, you can also edit screenshot using the same tools after saving the plain screenshot. In fact, the newest version of ShareX has a modernized image editing tool that lets you do all kinds of things, including adding custom frames and backgrounds to your screenshots, giving them rounded corners, and blurring out portions of the image, and more. There's a lot here to make your screenshots pop, and it looks great.

That's not all there is to it, either. In addition to screenshots, ShareX can also record video, including either system audio or microphone audio, and you even have the option to save short videos as GIFs, making them easier to embed on online forums and other sites. It's a very complete set of tools for capturing your own screen.

How to record your screen in Windows 11

Screen recording in Windows 11 can be accomplished in a few relatively easy ways. Our guide can walk you through each process, step by step.

By  João Carrasqueira

It even connects to internet services

Sharing is caring, after all

Beyond taking and editing screenshots, ShareX also offers sharing tools, and it does a surprisingly great job at that. There are multiple upload targets you can set. By default, it uses Imgur, since you can upload anonymously without an account. But you can also link accounts for places like ImageShack, Flickr, and Photobucket, and upload to those directly. You can set a default uploader of your choice, so once you choose to upload an image, it goes straight there without any more work.

You can even set custom file storage destinations, so you can upload images to cloud services like OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox, or even enterprise-oriented services like Amazon S3 and Backblaze B2 buckets.

And what's crazy is you're not even limited to images. As an upload tool, ShareX supports all kinds of files, and even text. You can drag and drop a .txt file onto ShareX and its content will be saved on Pastebin so you can share it with the world, complete with the ability to customize things such as expiry timers.

5 reasons you should use ShareX instead of Snipping Tool

ShareX provides more features for power users

2
By  Megan Ellis

Between the capturing and editing capabilities and the upload tools, there are so many pages of customization that it can feel overwhelming. But if you giuve yourself some time, it quickly becomes worth it.

Somehow, there's more

Bonus features make it even more versatile

In addition to the core features for capturing and sharing content, ShareX takes yet another step further and includes all sort of small bonus features that make it even more interesting. Not all of these really fit the theme of a screenshot tool, but there's a good chance you'll find some use for them, making ShareX even more invaluable.

One example is a video converter, which uses FFmpeg to transcode any video files you have. This may seem odd, but ShareX already uses FFmpeg to encode screen recordings, so this is a pretty natural extension of that.

5 features that make ShareX is the best screenshot tool you've never used

Level up your screenshot experience

By  João Carrasqueira

Otherwise, you can use ShareX to compare two images with a slider view, which also gives you a similarity score, you can use a color picker to copy hex values for any given color (either by using a color mixer or picking one from your screen), you can measure distances in pixels on your screen, combine or split images, and more. None of these are big selling points on their own but they're nice additions that make a great tool even better.

And because so many of these tools can be assigned to hotkeys, it becomes really easy to get to what you want in a flash without jumping through a million menus. You can customize it to fit your needs, which is wonderful.

It's not for everyone

Sometimes, the basics are good enough

As great as ShareX is, I'm not trying to say it's meant to be for everyone. As I've already mentioned, the seemingly endless customization options and tools available can make it feel overwhelming for new users, and it's a lot if you just want to take screenshots to share. Plus, ShareX has a UI that feels a little outdated, even if it is perfectly functional.

If you just want to take screenshots and be done with it, sticking with the Snipping Tool is a valid choice. It has a very modern look, and it can do all the basics, in addition to having some editing features of its own, and some extra capabilities like OCR and QR code recognition. In some ways, Snipping Tool is actually better, because its screen recordings can include both microphone and desktop audio, which ShareX doesn't do out of the box.

Still, the feature set in ShareX is immense, and it stands out as a great option for anyone who wants to get a little more out of their screenshots, on top of everything else it can do. It comes highly recommended, and it's such a lightweight app that it doesn't cost much to try.

item.title: I disabled the AM5 BIOS setting everyone uses, and my random crashes finally stopped
item.itunes:title: I disabled the AM5 BIOS setting everyone uses, and my random crashes finally stopped
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For weeks, I had been plagued by random crashes in one of my favorite games, and nothing about my system had changed. The symptoms of these crashes would vary between full system lockups, a sudden game freeze and closure, and even BSODs. Because nothing about my system had changed, I figured it was just the game itself acting up, but then the crashing started happening during desktop tasks as well, and I knew the cause was something deeper.

I suspected memory, and dropping my 64GB of DDR5 down from 6000MT/s to 5600MT/s solved the crashing, but I was giving up some performance. Months later, I had an epiphany—compared to DDR4, DDR5 tends to walk a much smaller tightrope of stability, balancing things like speed, voltage, and timings, and one of the things that helps keep things from spiraling into instability is the constant memory retraining that happens on boot. There's one setting on AM5 boards that gives you lightning-fast boot times, but sacrifices that lengthy retraining process, and it was the culprit.

These two motherboard settings could halve your AMD PC's boot time

That's less time spent looking at yourself in the screen.

5
By  Samarveer Singh

Memory Context Restore is the setting

A great BIOS setting for lowering AM5 boot times

Every time an AM5 system boots from scratch, the motherboard trains its memory. It runs a battery of read and write operations to tune signal timings and reference voltages until it finds settings the memory can reliably run at. With DDR5, especially at high capacities or with all four slots populated, that process is pretty slow, and AM5 earned a reputation for long boots early on because of it.

Memory Context Restore solves that by saving the results of a successful training run after POST and uses those for later boots, skipping the retraining process entirely. This cuts boot times significantly. MCR doesn't cause bad memory training, and if the initial training result had healthy margins, you get fast boots with no downsides. For most systems and most memory configurations, it's a non-issue, but for some systems, it can be the difference between serious instability and a rock-solid system.

I let the NVIDIA App overclock my GPU, and it left me impressed

For a "conservative" OC tool, the NVIDIA App gave me remarkable results

7
By  Samarveer Singh

Four sticks at 6000MT/s is actually a significant ask

My system is running two different kits, too

My memory setup made me a prime candidate for a marginal training result. I run two identical DDR5-6000 kits, 2x16GB each, for four DIMMs total. On AM5 that means two DIMMs per channel, which is the hardest configuration for the memory controller to drive. AMD's official spec for the 7800X3D is DDR5-5200 with two DIMMs, and just DDR5-3600 with four. Running four sticks at 6000 is well past what AMD guarantees. This is technically an overclock, even if an EXPO profile makes it a single toggle.

I bought two Crucial kits of the same model instead of one 64GB kit, and this can be a factor in instability as well. Separately purchased kits can use different memory ICs or PCB revisions under the same part number, and when you combine that with the already marginal memory configuration, there's not a lot of room for error.

Why memory tests passed just fine but games didn't

An extended long-term test would've caught it eventually, but games stress memory in different ways

Memory stress tests are where I expected to find the problem, but they all came out clean with relatively long runs. These aren't 24 hour tests, more like a few hours, but I figured that'd be long enough to weed out any potential instability. I was incorrect.

One of my favorite games, Escape From Tarkov, was crashing seemingly at random. Some nights I could play without a crash, but others, it'd be every 30 minutes or so. The most likely explanation is that Tarkov's workload, which is heavy on RAM and constant asset streaming, stresses the memory in ways a test pattern doesn't. A pass in TestMem5 or OCCT is strong evidence of stability, but it isn't proof, and when dropping the speed from 6000 to 5600 fixed things, it pointed to a training margin problem rather than bad hardware or anything else.

I armed spare PCIe slots with cheap NVMe adapters, and they were the best quality-of-life upgrade for my PCs

Filling the empty PCIe sockets with NVMe adapters was totally worth it

5
By  Ayush Pande

The cost: boot times

I now wait around 60 seconds for my system to boot

​​​​​​​

From the time I press the power button to the time I see the Windows login screen is around 60 seconds, give or take. About five of those seconds are my Limine bootloader waiting to auto-select Windows, so the extra memory training adds somewhere around 30 seconds to a cold boot. MCR seriously sped things along, but it's not all-or-nothing here.

I actually reflected for a moment on my power habits and found that I rarely shut down my computer anyway. The vast majority of the time it's either sitting on, idle, or in sleep mode. I really only wait for a cold boot when changing some settings, swapping operating systems, or returning from an extended time away.

I enabled Memory Context Restore, and my Ryzen boot times stopped being a joke

The only bad thing is I don't have time to make coffee while I wait

By  Joe Rice-Jones

If you're running DDR5 on AM5, MCR is a setting worth taking a closer look at

If you're running four sticks or mixed kits on AM5 and chasing crashes that memory tests won't reproduce, try turning off Memory Context Restore before you lower your EXPO speed. If the crashes continue, then dropping to a lower speed might be advisable, but there's always a possibility the cause isn't memory. For me, though, that one toggle was the difference between a system I couldn't trust and one I don't think about anymore, and it cost me about 25 seconds.

item.title: Every vibe-coding tool wants your subscription, but this one wants your bad ideas
item.itunes:title: Every vibe-coding tool wants your subscription, but this one wants your bad ideas
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Vibe coding tools have made building small apps pretty easy and more accessible than ever. All it takes is writing a prompt, technically. But I'd argue that the workspace you're in matters more than the ideas you have, because you'll eventually need to learn how to iterate, what a codebase is, and potentially how to publish your build. And the vibe coding tool you're using determines the quality of this experience.

Unfortunately, most of the good ones are paywalled or run on some type of credit system. This means that half the time you're paying before you even get to poke around and truly understand what you're building, so the dumb side project that had the potential to turn into something useful now never even gets a prompt. But I've found a free and open-source vibe-coding tool that's way more forgiving of your early, throwaway ideas, called Dyad…

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

Dyad is an app builder that lives on your computer

It doesn't feel like a restricted free trial

Dyad is a free, open-source AI app builder, and works similarly to tools like Lovable or Bolt. You describe the app in a chat and watch a working preview render next to it. Dyad runs on your own machine, and every file it generates gets saved to your disk as regular code. That code can go straight into VS Code or GitHub later. You don't even have to make an account to get it running, which I always appreciate about a tool.

The free version gives you almost the full product. There aren't any project limits, and Build mode, which does most of the work, has no usage caps for anyone. The paid Pro and Max plans ($20 and $79 a month) mostly add Dyad's own AI additions and Pro modes, but you don't need them for basic usage.

Like many vibe-coding tools, Dyad is meant for developers as much as non-developers. Dyad's creator actually says he enjoys helping non-developers build things they didn't think they could, and the entire pipeline runs through chat. I didn't write or touch a single line of code while testing it, though the code's right there and available to edit if you need to, or in my case, hand it off to someone who actually codes.

I replaced Claude Design with this open-source tool, and I'm not paying for design software again

Open Design is what everyone should be using.

14
By  Anurag Singh

You probably already pay for the AI it needs

Dyad's brilliant AI usage system

Dyad doesn't ship with its own AI, so you bring one. Local models are the fully free route. Ollama gets picked up automatically on localhost, as well as LM Studio, and anything else with an OpenAI-compatible API can be added as a custom provider. Dyad admits smaller local models can struggle with its instructions, so your VRAM will determine your experience with the local route here. Regular API keys cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and OpenRouter, which is the usual pay-per-token setup.

The newer option is the one I actually used. Since version 1.16, you can build with your ChatGPT subscription, even as a free Dyad user. As far as I can tell, usage comes out of the Codex allowance bundled with ChatGPT plans. Dyad itself just calls it your ChatGPT usage allowance, though. The optional Fast mode hints at how it works, since it uses twice as much of that allowance. I'm on ChatGPT Pro at the moment, so the pool goes pretty deep for me, and Free Dyad users don't pay Dyad anything extra beyond the usual free-tier limits.

You can still pick the exact model from your chosen provider and the reasoning effort yourself. At first I just stuck with GPT 5.6 Luna because it was all about experimenting initially. Dyad reckons this gets you up to 5x the usage of Pro credits alone, which I'll take their word on since I never bought any.

I just think this is overall a brilliant "payment" model. You hook up to the AI tools you already use and it pulls from that existing pool, so you're not paying anything extra. Or just go the local route to keep it completely free. This ultimately makes you more likely to expand on your dumb ideas because you don't have to watch every single credit like a hawk.

I switched from Claude Code to Codex for a week, and the trade-offs surprised me

One week, two tools, a lot of opinions.

29
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Plan it, then build it

Dyad holds your hand along the way

Plan mode is where you go with your half-baked ideas. You do not need to know exactly what you want or how it's even going to work, that's what this mode is for. I gave it a vague idea for a screen-time dashboard running on fake phone data, and it asked a short multiple-choice questionnaire before getting started. Once your plan is ready, you get the option to continue building in the same session or hop over to a fresh one with the plan.

The building happens in either Build mode or Basic Agent. Build now runs in a loop, checking the app and its own changes over several steps, and it's unlimited. The Agent can also catch and fix bugs on its own, but free users get 20 Agent messages a day. Once it's running you just watch it tick through its own to-do list file by file, and then the build will eventually run and your preview will start rendering in the split panel. Every edit saves a new version automatically, restoring an older one doesn't wipe anything, and the history stays intact.

The right side holds the live preview and the full codebase. Visual editing is locked to Pro, but you can select components in the preview and attach them to the chat. For example, I grabbed the category filter buttons and asked about them in Ask mode, and it gave me a full synthesis of the purpose of the buttons.

Once you're happy, you connect the app to GitHub from inside Dyad, and hitting Sync to GitHub pushes whatever's on your drive up to a repo. Dyad's own guide suggests Vercel from there, since it has a decent free plan. It rebuilds the app each time you sync, so the live link stays current.

I tried this underrated Google Labs tool to vibe-code my UI designs, and now I regret not using it sooner

Google's best-kept design tool

3
By  Nolen Jonker

A tool for the ideas you'd normally skip

That screen-time dashboard runs entirely on made-up data and will probably never leave my hard drive. It was just an experiment. And most of my designs and builds end up in a graveyard. But that's exactly the point with Dyad, that you get to experiment without having to worry about a credit pool draining.

Dyad

Unfortunately, most of the good ones are paywalled or run on some type of credit system. This means that half the time you're paying before you even get to poke around and truly understand what you're building, so the dumb side project that had the potential to turn into something useful now never even gets a prompt. But I've found a free and open-source vibe-coding tool that's way more forgiving of your early, throwaway ideas, called Dyad…

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

Dyad is an app builder that lives on your computer

It doesn't feel like a restricted free trial

Dyad is a free, open-source AI app builder, and works similarly to tools like Lovable or Bolt. You describe the app in a chat and watch a working preview render next to it. Dyad runs on your own machine, and every file it generates gets saved to your disk as regular code. That code can go straight into VS Code or GitHub later. You don't even have to make an account to get it running, which I always appreciate about a tool.

The free version gives you almost the full product. There aren't any project limits, and Build mode, which does most of the work, has no usage caps for anyone. The paid Pro and Max plans ($20 and $79 a month) mostly add Dyad's own AI additions and Pro modes, but you don't need them for basic usage.

Like many vibe-coding tools, Dyad is meant for developers as much as non-developers. Dyad's creator actually says he enjoys helping non-developers build things they didn't think they could, and the entire pipeline runs through chat. I didn't write or touch a single line of code while testing it, though the code's right there and available to edit if you need to, or in my case, hand it off to someone who actually codes.

I replaced Claude Design with this open-source tool, and I'm not paying for design software again

Open Design is what everyone should be using.

By  Anurag Singh

You probably already pay for the AI it needs

Dyad's brilliant AI usage system

Dyad doesn't ship with its own AI, so you bring one. Local models are the fully free route. Ollama gets picked up automatically on localhost, as well as LM Studio, and anything else with an OpenAI-compatible API can be added as a custom provider. Dyad admits smaller local models can struggle with its instructions, so your VRAM will determine your experience with the local route here. Regular API keys cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and OpenRouter, which is the usual pay-per-token setup.

As far as I can tell, usage comes out of the Codex allowance bundled with ChatGPT plans. Dyad itself just calls it your ChatGPT usage allowance, though. One week, two tools, a lot of opinions.

By  Mahnoor Faisal

Plan it, then build it

Dyad holds your hand along the way

Plan mode is where you go with your half-baked ideas. You do not need to know exactly what you want or how it's even going to work, that's what this mode is for. Once you're happy, you connect the app to GitHub from inside Dyad, and hitting Sync to GitHub pushes whatever's on your drive up to a repo. Dyad's own guide suggests Vercel from there, since it has a decent free plan. It rebuilds the app each time you sync, so the live link stays current.

I tried this underrated Google Labs tool to vibe-code my UI designs, and now I regret not using it sooner

Google's best-kept design tool

A tool for the ideas you'd normally skip

That screen-time dashboard runs entirely on made-up data and will probably never leave my hard drive. It was just an experiment. And most of my designs and builds end up in a graveyard. But that's exactly the point with Dyad, that you get to experiment without having to worry about a credit pool draining.

item.title: ChromeOS isn't dead yet, as Google says it'll support it until 2034
item.itunes:title: ChromeOS isn't dead yet, as Google says it'll support it until 2034
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Google moves from Chromebooks to Googlebooks, yet ChromeOS gets updates and security patches through mid‑2034.
  • Some newer Chromebooks will be eligible for a Googlebook OS upgrade or direct migration paths.
  • Chromebooks stay a safe, practical buy—regular security updates mean you can keep using them.

A little while ago, Google shook up the scene by announcing it would no longer produce ChromeOS devices. Instead, it was moving toward Googlebooks, which trades the Chromebook's affordability for raw on-board AI processing power. Fortunately, there is good news for Chromebook fans, as the company has revealed that it will continue supporting ChromeOS for another eight years.

ChromeOS will continue getting updates until 2034

There's a lot of life in your Chromebooks yet

Google announced the end-of-support date for ChromeOS on its Chrome Enterprise and Education Help webpage (via Engadget). Titled "What the Googlebook announcement means for your ChromeOS devices," Google explains what Chromebook owners can expect now that the Googlebook is taking over its spotlight.

It's pretty much all good news; Google will continue to honor its support plan, and people can continue using their Chromebooks like they always have. In fact, Google says some of the newer Chromebook devices will get an upgrade to Googlebook OS, with details coming soon.

However, if you scroll to the FAQ section of the article and expand the part that reads "How should this announcement impact our current hardware purchasing and refresh plans?", you find this little nugget:

"ChromeOS devices will continue to receive regular updates and security patches through mid-2034. For qualifying devices purchased today whose 10-year support lifecycle extends beyond 2034, Google is committed to supporting your transition to Googlebook OS, with many devices offering direct migration paths."

It's good to see that Google will continue to support ChromeOS, even after it threw out the Chromebook line to focus on its Googlebooks. It's a good indicator for anyone thinking of buying a Googlebook, at any rate.

The Googlebook is finally here, and aims to blend Android and ChromeOS into one premium laptop operating system

The first Googlebook laptops are coming from Acer, Asus Dell, and HP.

item.title: Someone got Super Mario 64 running on the SNES using the Super FX chip
item.itunes:title: Someone got Super Mario 64 running on the SNES using the Super FX chip
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Someone has gotten Super Mario 64 ported to SNES, showing off the FX chip's surprising power.
  • The engine is reworked to fit on the SNES, and assets look chunky but impressive for the hardware.
  • Not released yet — the creator will provide a download once it's polished and stable.

It's always fun to see how people get old games running on new hardware; just look at all the different ways people got Doom running on devices. But what if you did the reverse and got a newer game running on older hardware? One YouTuber has slowly been making their way through Nintendo's retro consoles, and this time, they got Super Mario 64 running off a SNES.

Super Mario 64 on the SNES shows how mighty the FX chip was

It's not perfect, but it's still very impressive

As spotted by Hackaday, this cool little feat was performed by Game of Tob on YouTube. The last time we saw them, they had managed to squeeze Minecraft onto the SNES, including a Nether portal that led to a very small, but still totally functional, version of the Nether. This time around, they managed to pack Super Mario 64 onto the SNES.

The actual engine needed a bit of rework, but in terms of in-game assets, this SNES version of Super Mario 64 keeps everything around, if not a little chunky-looking. It also needs to pretty aggressively cull the level to make sure everything fits on the hardware. Still, it's a really cool insight into what the SNES could achieve with its FX chip; who knows what kind of games Nintendo would have made if they stuck with the SNES instead of moving on to the N64?

Game of Tobi hasn't released the project just yet, but once they have ironed out all the problems and got it into a state where they're happy with it, you'll be able to download it and run it on your own SNES.

Someone got Minecraft running on a Game Boy Color, and so can you

It has a weirdly good framerate for a 3D Game Boy game.

1
By  Simon Batt

item.title: I tried replacing Proxmox with an open-source OS you’ve never heard of
item.itunes:title: I tried replacing Proxmox with an open-source OS you’ve never heard of
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve been a fan of Proxmox ever since I first used it with my first ever home server, and my admiration for this virtualization platform has only grown with each passing update. That said, I’m always looking for cool alternatives to try out, and I’ve already gone through everything from popular platforms like ESXi, XCP-ng, Unraid, and Windows Server 2019 to Harvester, ZimaOS, and other obscure PVE rivals.

So, you can imagine my enthusiasm when I heard ZStack released their virtualization platform, ZSVirt, under the GNU GPL 3.0 license last month. Since I’m already a fan of open-source utilities, I figured I could use it to replace an existing Proxmox node in my arsenal. And despite my initial hesitation, I had to admit that ZSVirt is an incredible option for a home lab, especially if you’re planning to configure full-fledged high-availability clusters.

Note: While I have some clusters in my arsenal, this article is written strictly from the POV of an average enthusiast, not someone who manages entire VM stacks for a living. As such, I’ll only cover ZSVirt’s perks and quirks from the lens of home labbers and average users instead of going over its utility in production-tier setups.

I tried moving my home lab off Proxmox multiple times, but nothing came close to replacing it

Proxmox is in a league of its own when it comes to home lab projects

3
By  Ayush Pande

It took me half an evening to get ZSVirt up and running

Even though the actual installation part didn’t take too long

Before I go over my experience with managing VMs via ZSVirt, let me go over the installation process. For the test rig, I decided to go with my Ryzen 5 1600 system, as it sets a decent baseline for the types of outdated machines I often convert into functioning home lab nodes. Besides the first-gen Ryzen processor, the PC has 16GB of DDR4 memory and a GTX 1080, which I often use for Proxmox experiments.

Anyway, the installation process went fairly smoothly. Once my PC booted into the installation wizard, I tweaked the user account, password, and storage settings before giving it the A-OK to overwrite my SSD with ZSVirt files. Just like Proxmox, the installation process took about 15 minutes, but little did I know, this was only the first part of the configuration sequence. Once the PC restarted into the ZSVirt boot drive, it took well over thirty minutes to get the sanity checks and package updates out of the way, and only then was I cleared to access the web UI.

However, once I’d logged into the online interface, I realized I’d have to go through yet another configuration process for my ZSVirt server. I’d set my PC as the management node earlier, so I had to choose the cluster, host, storage, and network settings. Credit where it’s due, ZSVirt has extensive documentation on the official website, including recommended settings for non-HA cluster setups such as mine. But if we were to compare it with the straightforward setup sequence on Proxmox, ZSVirt’s configuration process is quite the hassle. But when I started creating VMs with ZSVirt, I quickly realized it was worth the extra effort…

ZSVirt is laden with all sorts of home lab features

Its management UI is extremely detailed

I often praise Proxmox for its detailed virtual machine management features, and ZSVirt is no slouch on this front, either. Personally, I think its UI is a tad more difficult to navigate for the average user, as some of the advanced options remain hidden inside a maze of menus. But once I went through the official docs, controlling my VMs became a lot smoother.

On the virtual machine front, I can change the resource allocation, console, authentication, and boot settings as I please, and it even includes VMTools to enhance the performance of my virtual guests and enable file-sharing between them and the host hardware. Plus, ZSVirt ships with enough PCI passthrough, resource monitoring, and event logging provisions to satisfy hardcore home labbers.

Unlike XCP-ng, which restricts backups on the free, pre-compiled version of its XOA management UI, ZSVirt lets me create backups and snapshots of my virtual machines directly from its web interface. The host settings are just as extensive, and I really appreciate that ZSVirt has an entire tab dedicated to logging and monitoring my systems. I’ll admit that the data and image storage pools were a bit difficult to configure, especially since I’m accustomed to Proxmox handling everything after the initial installation sequence.

ZSVirt also has terrific cluster provisions

Since we’re on the subject of multiple servers, ZSVirt has a plethora of cluster management tools. The main dashboard is a lot akin to Proxmox Datacenter Manager, as it displays the overarching VM metrics, resource utilization stats, and alerts from my clusters. On the network front alone, I can tinker with distributed port groups, topology charts, uplink configurations, and cluster settings. Similarly, ZSVirt supports NFS and distributed storage pools as well as iSCSI, FC, and other LUN solutions for the data pools, which are handy for HA clusters.

The DRS, VM scheduling, and high-availability policies are just as easy to tweak on ZSVirt, and I love that it tracks the actual and overcommitted resource statistics for all cluster nodes. Heck, ZSVirt natively supports Terraform automation pipelines, something that requires additional plugins on Proxmox. Combine that with its straightforward VM migration tools, and it’s an incredible option for cluster-heavy home labs.

I tried building a home lab with Hyper-V as a Proxmox user – here's how it went

Hyper-V may be far from perfect, but it's pretty decent for newcomers to the home labbing scene

11
By  Ayush Pande

That said, ZSVirt can’t replace good ol’ Proxmox for my projects

PVE is just that good for ordinary home labs such as mine

Despite all its perks, I have to admit that ZSVirt can’t replace Proxmox for my home lab. Sure, its cluster management and virtualization provisions are top-notch, but if I wanted to deploy containers, I’d have to rely on nested setups involving resource-hogging VMs. In contrast, Proxmox lets me spin up FOSS services as LXCs, with the PVE Community Scripts repo making this process as simple as running a single command.

ZSVirt also needs at least 8GB of RAM on the host system, while Proxmox just needs 1GB for the virtualization platform. In a time when RAM prices have hit unhinged levels, I’d have an easier time repurposing old machines as container-hosting platforms with Proxmox than ZSVirt. Not to mention, ZSVirt has a steeper learning curve than Proxmox, and even with the stellar official documentation, it can’t compete with the massive community support you’ll find in the PVE ecosystem.

I’ve been a fan of Proxmox ever since I first used it with my first ever home server, and my admiration for this virtualization platform has only grown with each passing update. That said, I’m always looking for cool alternatives to try out, and I’ve already gone through everything from popular platforms like ESXi, XCP-ng, Unraid, and Windows Server 2019 to Harvester, ZimaOS, and other obscure PVE rivals.

So, you can imagine my enthusiasm when I heard ZStack released their virtualization platform, ZSVirt, under the GNU GPL 3.0 license last month. Since I’m already a fan of open-source utilities, I figured I could use it to replace an existing Proxmox node in my arsenal. And despite my initial hesitation, I had to admit that ZSVirt is an incredible option for a home lab, especially if you’re planning to configure full-fledged high-availability clusters.

Note: While I have some clusters in my arsenal, this article is written strictly from the POV of an average enthusiast, not someone who manages entire VM stacks for a living. As such, I’ll only cover ZSVirt’s perks and quirks from the lens of home labbers and average users instead of going over its utility in production-tier setups.

I tried moving my home lab off Proxmox multiple times, but nothing came close to replacing it

Proxmox is in a league of its own when it comes to home lab projects

3
By  Ayush Pande

It took me half an evening to get ZSVirt up and running

Even though the actual installation part didn’t take too long

Before I go over my experience with managing VMs via ZSVirt, let me go over the installation process. For the test rig, I decided to go with my Ryzen 5 1600 system, as it sets a decent baseline for the types of outdated machines I often convert into functioning home lab nodes. Besides the first-gen Ryzen processor, the PC has 16GB of DDR4 memory and a GTX 1080, which I often use for Proxmox experiments.

Anyway, the installation process went fairly smoothly. Once my PC booted into the installation wizard, I tweaked the user account, password, and storage settings before giving it the A-OK to overwrite my SSD with ZSVirt files. Just like Proxmox, the installation process took about 15 minutes, but little did I know, this was only the first part of the configuration sequence. Once the PC restarted into the ZSVirt boot drive, it took well over thirty minutes to get the sanity checks and package updates out of the way, and only then was I cleared to access the web UI.

However, once I’d logged into the online interface, I realized I’d have to go through yet another configuration process for my ZSVirt server. I’d set my PC as the management node earlier, so I had to choose the cluster, host, storage, and network settings. Credit where it’s due, ZSVirt has extensive documentation on the official website, including recommended settings for non-HA cluster setups such as mine. But if we were to compare it with the straightforward setup sequence on Proxmox, ZSVirt’s configuration process is quite the hassle. But when I started creating VMs with ZSVirt, I quickly realized it was worth the extra effort…

ZSVirt is laden with all sorts of home lab features

Its management UI is extremely detailed

I often praise Proxmox for its detailed virtual machine management features, and ZSVirt is no slouch on this front, either. Personally, I think its UI is a tad more difficult to navigate for the average user, as some of the advanced options remain hidden inside a maze of menus. But once I went through the official docs, controlling my VMs became a lot smoother.

On the virtual machine front, I can change the resource allocation, console, authentication, and boot settings as I please, and it even includes VMTools to enhance the performance of my virtual guests and enable file-sharing between them and the host hardware. Plus, ZSVirt ships with enough PCI passthrough, resource monitoring, and event logging provisions to satisfy hardcore home labbers.

Unlike XCP-ng, which restricts backups on the free, pre-compiled version of its XOA management UI, ZSVirt lets me create backups and snapshots of my virtual machines directly from its web interface. The host settings are just as extensive, and I really appreciate that ZSVirt has an entire tab dedicated to logging and monitoring my systems. I’ll admit that the data and image storage pools were a bit difficult to configure, especially since I’m accustomed to Proxmox handling everything after the initial installation sequence.

ZSVirt also has terrific cluster provisions

Since we’re on the subject of multiple servers, ZSVirt has a plethora of cluster management tools. The main dashboard is a lot akin to Proxmox Datacenter Manager, as it displays the overarching VM metrics, resource utilization stats, and alerts from my clusters. On the network front alone, I can tinker with distributed port groups, topology charts, uplink configurations, and cluster settings. Similarly, ZSVirt supports NFS and distributed storage pools as well as iSCSI, FC, and other LUN solutions for the data pools, which are handy for HA clusters.

The DRS, VM scheduling, and high-availability policies are just as easy to tweak on ZSVirt, and I love that it tracks the actual and overcommitted resource statistics for all cluster nodes. Heck, ZSVirt natively supports Terraform automation pipelines, something that requires additional plugins on Proxmox. Combine that with its straightforward VM migration tools, and it’s an incredible option for cluster-heavy home labs.

I tried building a home lab with Hyper-V as a Proxmox user – here's how it went

Hyper-V may be far from perfect, but it's pretty decent for newcomers to the home labbing scene

11
By  Ayush Pande

That said, ZSVirt can’t replace good ol’ Proxmox for my projects

PVE is just that good for ordinary home labs such as mine

Despite all its perks, I have to admit that ZSVirt can’t replace Proxmox for my home lab. Sure, its cluster management and virtualization provisions are top-notch, but if I wanted to deploy containers, I’d have to rely on nested setups involving resource-hogging VMs. In contrast, Proxmox lets me spin up FOSS services as LXCs, with the PVE Community Scripts repo making this process as simple as running a single command.

ZSVirt also needs at least 8GB of RAM on the host system, while Proxmox just needs 1GB for the virtualization platform. In a time when RAM prices have hit unhinged levels, I’d have an easier time repurposing old machines as container-hosting platforms with Proxmox than ZSVirt. Not to mention, ZSVirt has a steeper learning curve than Proxmox, and even with the stellar official documentation, it can’t compete with the massive community support you’ll find in the PVE ecosystem.

item.itunes:title: PewDiePie's free self-hosted image editor does what Adobe and Canva charge for
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most editing tools worth your while come with a subscription attached, unfortunately. And now that most of them are AI-powered, it's used to justify increased pricing and more paywalls. There's also the issue of your work sitting on servers you don't own. Photoshop's Generative Fill is processed on Adobe's cloud servers, with each generation pulling a credit from a monthly allotment tied to your plan. Canva does something similar with its one-click background remover, which isn't on the free tier and only comes with Pro.

Luckily, self-hosted tools have been creeping into this AI-powered image editing and design space. One of the more unlikely places it's turned up is Odysseus, the AI workspace PewDiePie released this year, which has an image editor tucked inside with a lot of the same AI tool names you'd find in Adobe's and Canva's menus. And it all runs on your own hardware…

This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me

I didn't expect it to replace my entire Adobe setup

13
By  Nolen Jonker

PewDiePie's AI workspace has an image editor hiding in it

He wanted to build his own Photoshop and make it free

PewDiePie (Felix Kjellberg) put Odysseus out as a free, self-hosted AI workspace, and it's grown a lot since launch. The GitHub org has since been renamed from pewdiepie-archdaemon to odysseus-dev, and the repo is sitting at almost 90k stars now. Most of this workspace focuses on chat, agents, and research. And the gallery and image editor kind of get lumped in under "extras". But I'd say this is one of the more interesting parts of the tool.

His reasons for building it are mostly about privacy. He's talked about how much personal info ends up with these companies and gets traded around between them, and he's promised the project will never cost money. He's also said he doesn't want AI doing the work for him but rather just help out when asked, which lines up with how the image editor also works.

The editor is where he's been the most ambitious, though. He's said outright that he's building his own Photoshop, while admitting it's far from as robust. Everything runs locally in Docker, with a section called the Cookbook handling model downloads and checking what your hardware can run.

I regret paying for Adobe Photoshop - this free tool is open-source and powerful

New king of open-source photo editing

5
By  Parth Shah

The Gallery doubles as a browser-based photo editor

The vibe reminds me a bit of Photopea crossed with Google Photos

When you open the Gallery for the first time, it looks a little like Google Photos. That's because it's a photo library first, with albums and tags, and dropping in a whole folder creates an album with its name. From there, you simply double-click a photo and hit edit to open it in the editor. But you can also start the editor from a blank canvas, which gives you the standard default pixel ratios.

The tool rail down the left is pretty familiar if you've used Photopea or Photoshop at all. Crop and transform sit up top with the move tool, and the brush and eraser come after that, with clone, lasso, and a magic wand further down. The AI tools are grouped at the very bottom with little sparkle icons. Along the top there's undo and redo plus a full history panel. This is all pretty standard stuff, so the functions themselves aren't exactly mind-blowing, but that's the whole point - simply having a solid, usable editor on your own terms. Plus, the interface is quite aesthetically pretty and also easy to navigate, and I always give a tool bonus points for that.

On the right there's a Photoshop-style stacking panel where each piece gets its own visibility toggle and opacity slider, and you can reorder them or add new ones. Each piece's image data, position, and opacity get saved with the project, and unfinished work is kept as a draft on the server so you can resume it later, even from another device. When you're done, you can overwrite the original in the gallery or save a new one.

There's a little ALPHA badge in the top-left corner of the editor, so it's still an early build, and you can kind of tell in some spots. For cropping something for socials or cloning out a little speck in an image, I'd say it's pretty decent, though.

I replaced Adobe, Figma, and Canva with ChatGPT and one open-source tool

Girl math says this counts as three cancelled subscriptions

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

The AI tools come in two very different sizes

Some need a GPU, some are happy on a CPU

The AI side comes in two pretty different sizes, and the size ends up deciding what you can actually run. Generative models paint new pixels from a text prompt, while the smaller tools each handle a single job.

For generative fill, my build only offered local Stable Diffusion models from the Cookbook (I tried plugging in an OpenAI key first, which the editor just ignored). One is an inpainting model trained specifically to fill a masked area, with extra inputs added for the mask itself. The other is Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, which has 2.5 billion parameters and needs around 9.9 GB of VRAM, not counting the text encoders.

For reference, the standard Docker setup doesn't give Odysseus access to your GPU, so on my machine everything ran on the CPU, and the inpainting download alone was past 9 GB after half an hour. So I hit yet another wall. But I wasn't out of luck…

The smaller tools live in the Cookbook's Dependencies tab. Background removal comes from rembg, which uses small ONNX models that download automatically the first time you run it. The Denoise and Upscale tools need realesrgan, based on Tencent ARC Lab's Real-ESRGAN, which was trained on purely synthetic data to restore real-world images. And click-to-select comes from sam_mask, built on Meta's Segment Anything, which relies on PyTorch and transformers being installed.

These are all a fraction of the size and ran fine on my CPU. The one-click install for rembg did hang on me though, and I had to finish it with a single pip command in PowerShell. But they all ended up working fine, and my favorite was probably the Sharpen AI tool just because of how on par it was with its paid counterparts. Features like free background removal on pretty much any machine is close to what PewDiePie was going for, so I count this as a success even though I didn't have any luck running the larger models.

I replaced Adobe, Figma, and Canva with one free tool, and I'm not paying for design software again

It's an all-kill design tool

15
By  Nolen Jonker

Where PewDiePie's image editor stands for now

A full Photoshop replacement is probably still a long way off, and PewDiePie is upfront about that. What I think Odysseus has got right is the boring middle, so stuff like background removal that many pay a monthly fee for. Generative fill is still waiting on hardware I don't have, but it costs nothing and works offline, so I'm fine with leaving that out for now.

item.title: Claude Code built the features I've been asking for in my favorite app, and it took 30 minutes
item.itunes:title: Claude Code built the features I've been asking for in my favorite app, and it took 30 minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Karakeep is one of the apps I use every day, and I’ve wanted to add a few things to it for years. I wanted to keep sources, notes, and highlights together around a story, ask questions about what I’ve saved, and compare articles that answer the same question differently. Having all that inside the app where I already save everything makes so much sense.

I recently asked Claude Code to add those features to Karakeep, and I now have a version with five extras built around my research needs. Along with projects, questions, and source comparisons, it connects saved items through the people and companies they mention and brings back older bookmarks when they’re relevant to my current research. The experience has been a lot better with those features in place.

My research now has a place in Karakeep

Everything I’m looking into stays together

When I’m researching a topic, I want to keep track of more than the links I’ve saved. There’s the question I’m trying to answer, the notes I’ve made, and specific passages that are relevant. I wanted somewhere in Karakeep to keep those things together, with enough context to understand where the research stands when I come back to it.

I asked Claude Code to add a Research Projects section that lets me group bookmarks, notes, highlights, and sources around a specific story. For instance, instead of collecting everything under a broad topic like local AI, I can create a project around whether a local model is good enough for everyday coding tasks. That project could include documentation, reviews, my own notes, and passages highlighted in saved articles.

The summary gives me somewhere to describe the current findings and what still needs an answer. I can update it as the research develops and use the status to distinguish work that’s ongoing from stories I’ve finished.

This chrome extension changed how I feed data to NotebookLM (and all my AI tools)

This tiny tool fixed my biggest AI workflow pain point.

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

I can ask questions and compare the answers

I can ask questions, then check the sources

If I’ve saved several reviews of a laptop, I want to be able to ask what they say about its battery life without opening each review and hunting through it. The information is already in my bookmarks, and I wanted Karakeep to help me find it.

I asked Claude Code to add Ask My Library, which lets me ask questions across everything I’ve saved. The answers include citations linking directly to the supporting bookmarks or passages, so I can check where a detail came from and read more if I need to. The same feature works for questions about saved recipes, travel guides, tutorials, or anything else in the collection.

I also added source comparison because getting an answer from several bookmarks doesn’t necessarily mean those bookmarks agree. I can select multiple articles and have Karakeep identify shared points, conflicting claims, different numbers, and information that only one source includes. With laptop reviews, for example, that could help me spot different battery-life results or a complaint that appears in only one review.

Older bookmarks become useful again

Even the ones I forgot saving

I also had Claude Code add automatic entity extraction, which identifies the people, companies, products, and places mentioned in saved items. I can click an entity to see everything I've collected about it. For example, Apple can appear in articles saved for several different stories, giving me a way to bring those sources together without organizing each story around the company itself.

I can save a product review for one project and an interview with its founder for another. Both contain information about the same company, even though I saved them for different reasons. Opening that company’s entity page brings those items into the same view. This also works for individual products, people, and places, so I can explore those connections across the collection.

I also wanted older material to come back when it’s relevant to something I’m currently saving or researching. That’s what Smart Resurfacing adds. For example, if I’m saving information about a place I want to visit, it can bring back an older travel guide about that destination.

Claude Code got it done in under an hour

Claude Code didn’t struggle with building any of these features, and the whole thing took around 30 to 45 minutes using Opus 5.5. Since Karakeep is open source and supports self-hosting, I had no difficulty forking it, adding the features, and running my modified version on my device.

I considered using Fable, but the less expensive Opus 5.5 handled everything. Its token pricing is lower than Fable’s, although I still exceeded the included usage limit on my $100-a-month Max plan during the build.

The Claude feature everyone ignores is the one I use every single day to boost my productivity

The ultimate Claude power-user trick

Karakeep is one of the apps I use every day, and I’ve wanted to add a few things to it for years. I wanted to keep sources, notes, and highlights together around a story, ask questions about what I’ve saved, and compare articles that answer the same question differently. Having all that inside the app where I already save everything makes so much sense.

I recently asked Claude Code to add those features to Karakeep, and I now have a version with five extras built around my research needs. Along with projects, questions, and source comparisons, it connects saved items through the people and companies they mention and brings back older bookmarks when they’re relevant to my current research. The experience has been a lot better with those features in place.

My research now has a place in Karakeep

Everything I’m looking into stays together

When I’m researching a topic, I want to keep track of more than the links I’ve saved. There’s the question I’m trying to answer, the notes I’ve made, and specific passages that are relevant. I wanted somewhere in Karakeep to keep those things together, with enough context to understand where the research stands when I come back to it.

I asked Claude Code to add a Research Projects section that lets me group bookmarks, notes, highlights, and sources around a specific story. For instance, instead of collecting everything under a broad topic like local AI, I can create a project around whether a local model is good enough for everyday coding tasks. That project could include documentation, reviews, my own notes, and passages highlighted in saved articles.

The summary gives me somewhere to describe the current findings and what still needs an answer. I can update it as the research develops and use the status to distinguish work that’s ongoing from stories I’ve finished.

This chrome extension changed how I feed data to NotebookLM (and all my AI tools)

This tiny tool fixed my biggest AI workflow pain point.

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

I can ask questions and compare the answers

I can ask questions, then check the sources

If I’ve saved several reviews of a laptop, I want to be able to ask what they say about its battery life without opening each review and hunting through it. The information is already in my bookmarks, and I wanted Karakeep to help me find it.

I asked Claude Code to add Ask My Library, which lets me ask questions across everything I’ve saved. The answers include citations linking directly to the supporting bookmarks or passages, so I can check where a detail came from and read more if I need to. The same feature works for questions about saved recipes, travel guides, tutorials, or anything else in the collection.

I also added source comparison because getting an answer from several bookmarks doesn’t necessarily mean those bookmarks agree. I can select multiple articles and have Karakeep identify shared points, conflicting claims, different numbers, and information that only one source includes. With laptop reviews, for example, that could help me spot different battery-life results or a complaint that appears in only one review.

Older bookmarks become useful again

Even the ones I forgot saving

I also had Claude Code add automatic entity extraction, which identifies the people, companies, products, and places mentioned in saved items. I can click an entity to see everything I've collected about it. For example, Apple can appear in articles saved for several different stories, giving me a way to bring those sources together without organizing each story around the company itself.

I can save a product review for one project and an interview with its founder for another. Both contain information about the same company, even though I saved them for different reasons. Opening that company’s entity page brings those items into the same view. This also works for individual products, people, and places, so I can explore those connections across the collection.

I also wanted older material to come back when it’s relevant to something I’m currently saving or researching. That’s what Smart Resurfacing adds. For example, if I’m saving information about a place I want to visit, it can bring back an older travel guide about that destination.

Claude Code got it done in under an hour

Claude Code didn’t struggle with building any of these features, and the whole thing took around 30 to 45 minutes using Opus 5.5. Since Karakeep is open source and supports self-hosting, I had no difficulty forking it, adding the features, and running my modified version on my device.

I considered using Fable, but the less expensive Opus 5.5 handled everything. Its token pricing is lower than Fable’s, although I still exceeded the included usage limit on my $100-a-month Max plan during the build.

The Claude feature everyone ignores is the one I use every single day to boost my productivity

item.itunes:summary:
This year has been the year of vibe-coding tools - or rather vibe-designing, vibe-prototyping, prompt-to-prototype, whatever you want to call it. It's probably safe to say that Replit and Lovable have been leading the pack, though I actually only started giving them a real shot after Claude Design happened, which was my true first impression of a vibe-design tool.

But there's a whole world of these tools to explore and you'd be doing yourself a disservice not to. One of the best options for vibe-coding has been hiding inside Google this whole time, and it's existed for three years now! I'd completely overlooked it, and regret not giving it a spin sooner…

What Google AI Studio actually is

It's been hiding in plain sight this whole time

Google AI Studio is a browser workspace for Gemini. There's a Playground where you test models, but Build mode is where you make actual apps, and it's pretty clearly the part Google cares about most right now. Since a March 2026 overhaul it's been a free, full-stack environment aimed at anyone, coding background or not, and it can make web apps or native Android apps straight from a prompt.

The free plan gets a modest quota without requiring your card. Free-tier content goes toward improving Google's products, though, so I'd keep anything private out of it. I already pay for Google AI Pro, and Pro and Ultra now come with higher AI Studio limits plus the premium models, but only inside the AI Studio web interface itself. The API key is more of a backup for when that daily allowance runs out, and it switches you over to pay-per-request.

The Antigravity part confused me a little at first. The agent building your app in Build mode runs on Antigravity's agent harness. But the Antigravity Agent Preview in the Playground is a separate thing that needs a paid API key Google AI plans don't cover, and Google's own docs warn a single prompt can eat an unbounded number of tokens, so I simply stopped poking around there and stuck with Build.

I used Claude Code, Google Antigravity, and Codex for a month and I have a clear winner for you

The search for the perfect coding assistant

32
By  Parth Shah

Going from a blank prompt to a working app

What building actually looks like in Google AI Studio

There isn't a feature that specifically says "build mode" in Google Studio, you simply enter build mode by hitting the "New app" button. You describe an app, and it writes a React front end with a Node.js server behind it while a live preview fills in on the right. You don't have to start from blank, though - you can remix something from the app gallery instead. I actually had a fun time experimenting with the gallery templates because it gives you a good sense of how others structure good apps. There's also a GitHub import if you've already got the code.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is the default model in mine, with older Flash versions tucked into a dropdown. The Pro models are part of what the paid plans unlock. Once you start prompting, you'll see it carries a lot more than it looks like. You can upload files for reference, and AI Chips let you bolt on features like image generation or Google Maps data onto whatever you're describing. There are also other Google integrations like Drive and Gmail, and AI Studio sorts out the sign-in permissions for those on its own. If your ideas involve logins, it'll offer to set up Firebase too.

My test was an app idea I've been toying with that gives you a broad-spectrum overview of your entire mobile app collection, including categories, time spent, battery usage, notification data, and so on. This already exists in apps like Screen Time and Digital Wellbeing, but there are a few extras I'd like to see included, so I tried my own. It only took about four minutes on 3.8 Flash and I had a working dashboard with a toggle that wraps it into a phone frame.

I replaced Claude Design with this open-source tool, and I'm not paying for design software again

Open Design is what everyone should be using.

14
By  Anurag Singh

There's a manual editor

And you walk away with the whole codebase

Every time a build finishes, it leaves a few suggestion cards under the chat, for example Add usage heat map or Add usage streaks, each tagged with what sort of change it'd be. I tried the streaks one and it went off and edited four files on its own.

There's also a manual editor in the renderer with a decent selection of tools. You can click anything in the preview and a small toolbar will pop up where you can change its color, with a proper hex picker, border and type settings, the works. This means you don't have to tinker with the code at all to make tweaks.

My favorite bit is how selecting anything drops it into your prompt as a chip, so instead of explaining which button I mean, I just select it (or a whole group of elements) and describe the change. When I asked it to tone down my neon app icons, it came back with a breakdown of every style it touched, hex codes included. V0 actually has something similar, but this is the version I've actually enjoyed using. Every change gets a checkpoint with a restore button too.

The code tab is what makes this more than a design tool. The whole codebase sits there and you can edit it right in the browser. I can't read most of it, however. Export covers GitHub, a ZIP download, and Export to Antigravity, which launched at I/O this year. I already use Antigravity, so staying inside Google's ecosystem is nice, though it doesn't carry over the chat history.

Publishing is free for your first two apps if you've never set up Google Cloud billing, and you can pick a custom ai.studio address. Shared apps run their Gemini calls against your own usage limits, too.

I tried this underrated Google Labs tool to vibe-code my UI designs, and now I regret not using it sooner

Google's best-kept design tool

3
By  Nolen Jonker

Not bad for a company that doesn't really do design

It's a little funny that the most fun I've had with a design-ish tool this year came from a company that doesn't really do design. To be fair, AI Studio is a coding tool first, and the design side came along with it. Claude Design is built more around polished slides and one-pagers, and I think it's good at those. When I want something that actually runs though, I have to say Google AI Studio seems to be a better option, plus you can run it without a subscription.

Google AI Studio
